subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Other intestinal disorders: ischemia, angiodysplasia, ileus, obstruction, SIBO
vignette: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden, severe abdominal pain that is dramatic relative to his benign abdominal examination. He later passes dark red 'currant jelly' stools. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 19,000/µL, and CT shows poor enhancement of the small bowel with a filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Chronic mesenteric ischemia with intestinal angina
Colonic ischemia at the splenic flexure watershed
Acute mesenteric ischemia from embolic SMA occlusion
Angiodysplasia of the right colon
Adhesive small bowel obstruction

explanation_correct: Acute mesenteric ischemia is a critical blockage of intestinal blood flow, often from embolic occlusion of the SMA, producing small bowel necrosis. It causes abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings and may produce red currant jelly stools. Atrial fibrillation, peripheral arterial disease, recent MI, and CHF are risk factors, matching this patient's presentation and embolic source.

explanation_incorrect.A: Chronic mesenteric ischemia produces postprandial epigastric pain ('intestinal angina') with food aversion and weight loss from atherosclerotic narrowing, not sudden pain out of proportion with an embolic SMA defect.
explanation_incorrect.B: Colonic ischemia at the splenic flexure causes crampy pain followed by hematochezia with a thumbprint sign in older adults, not an SMA filling defect with severe pain out of proportion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Angiodysplasia causes painless hematochezia from tortuous right colon vessels, often with aortic stenosis or von Willebrand disease, not acute severe pain and an SMA embolus.
explanation_incorrect.E: Adhesive small bowel obstruction causes colicky pain, vomiting, and air-fluid levels after prior surgery, not pain out of proportion with an arterial filling defect.

educationalObjective: Acute mesenteric ischemia from SMA embolism causes pain out of proportion to exam and currant jelly stools, with atrial fibrillation as a key risk factor.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Other intestinal disorders: ischemia, angiodysplasia, ileus, obstruction, SIBO
vignette: A 78-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presents with several episodes of painless bright red blood per rectum. Colonoscopy shows no diverticula or malignancy, but angiography demonstrates tortuous, dilated vessels in the right colon that are oozing contrast. He also has calcific aortic stenosis.
question: Which of the following is the most likely source of this patient's bleeding?

options.text: Angiodysplasia of the right colon
Diverticulosis of the sigmoid colon
Acute mesenteric ischemia from an SMA embolus
Colonic ischemia at a watershed area
A Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa

explanation_correct: Angiodysplasia is tortuous dilation of vessels that causes hematochezia, most often in the right colon and in older patients. It is confirmed by angiography, which shows the characteristic dilated, tortuous vessels. Associations include end-stage renal disease, von Willebrand disease, and aortic stenosis—all consistent with this patient's presentation of painless bleeding.

explanation_incorrect.B: Sigmoid diverticulosis causes painless hematochezia from vasa recta rupture but is left-sided and would show diverticula on colonoscopy, not tortuous right colon vessels on angiography.
explanation_incorrect.C: Acute mesenteric ischemia from an SMA embolus causes severe pain out of proportion to exam and currant jelly stools, not isolated painless bleeding with angiodysplastic vessels.
explanation_incorrect.D: Colonic ischemia at a watershed causes crampy pain then hematochezia with a thumbprint sign, not painless bleeding from dilated right colon vessels.
explanation_incorrect.E: Meckel diverticulum causes painless bleeding from ectopic gastric mucosa in the ileum, typically in children, and would be detected by a pertechnetate scan, not right colon angiography.

educationalObjective: Angiodysplasia causes painless hematochezia from tortuous right colon vessels in older patients, associated with ESRD, von Willebrand disease, and aortic stenosis.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Other intestinal disorders: ischemia, angiodysplasia, ileus, obstruction, SIBO
vignette: A 66-year-old man with hyperlipidemia and smoking history reports dull epigastric pain that begins about 30 minutes after meals and lasts for hours. He has begun eating less and has lost 8 kg over 3 months. Atherosclerosis is noted in the celiac and superior mesenteric arteries. His abdomen is soft and nontender between meals.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's postprandial pain and weight loss?

options.text: Embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery with bowel infarction
Gastric ulcer disease from Helicobacter pylori infection
Irritable bowel syndrome with altered bowel habits
Pancreatic adenocarcinoma with painless jaundice
Atherosclerotic narrowing of the celiac artery and SMA causing intestinal hypoperfusion

explanation_correct: Chronic mesenteric ischemia, or 'intestinal angina,' results from atherosclerosis of the celiac artery, SMA (most commonly affected), or IMA, causing intestinal hypoperfusion. It produces postprandial epigastric pain because blood flow cannot meet the increased demand of digestion, leading to food aversion and weight loss. This patient's vascular risk factors and eating-related pain are classic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Embolic SMA occlusion causes acute mesenteric ischemia with sudden pain out of proportion, not chronic postprandial pain with food aversion over months.
explanation_incorrect.B: H. pylori ulcer disease causes epigastric pain related to meals but would not be explained by celiac and SMA atherosclerosis or produce the intestinal angina pattern with severe food aversion.
explanation_incorrect.C: Irritable bowel syndrome causes recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation and stool changes without structural disease; it does not cause atherosclerotic vascular findings or this postprandial hypoperfusion pattern.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma classically causes painless jaundice and weight loss, not reproducible postprandial epigastric pain tied to intestinal blood flow.

educationalObjective: Chronic mesenteric ischemia (intestinal angina) from atherosclerosis causes postprandial epigastric pain, food aversion, and weight loss.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Other intestinal disorders: ischemia, angiodysplasia, ileus, obstruction, SIBO
vignette: A 70-year-old woman develops crampy abdominal pain followed by bright red blood per rectum. CT shows segmental bowel wall thickening and mucosal hemorrhage at the splenic flexure, with a 'thumbprint' appearance from mucosal edema and hemorrhage. She has a history of hypertension and diabetes.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Acute mesenteric ischemia from an SMA embolus
Colonic ischemia at a watershed area
Angiodysplasia of the right colon
Chronic mesenteric ischemia with intestinal angina
Ischemic necrosis of the terminal ileum in a premature infant

explanation_correct: Colonic ischemia typically occurs at watershed areas such as the splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction, where perfusion is most tenuous. It causes crampy abdominal pain followed by hematochezia, usually in older adults, and imaging shows a thumbprint sign from mucosal edema and hemorrhage. This patient's pain, bleeding, location, and imaging are classic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Acute mesenteric ischemia from SMA embolism causes severe pain out of proportion to findings with small bowel necrosis, not segmental splenic flexure disease with a thumbprint sign.
explanation_incorrect.C: Angiodysplasia causes painless hematochezia from tortuous right colon vessels confirmed by angiography, not crampy pain with thumbprinting at a watershed area.
explanation_incorrect.D: Chronic mesenteric ischemia produces chronic postprandial epigastric pain with food aversion and weight loss, not acute crampy pain and hematochezia with thumbprinting.
explanation_incorrect.E: Necrotizing enterocolitis affects premature formula-fed infants with pneumatosis and portal venous gas, not a 70-year-old with splenic flexure ischemia.

educationalObjective: Colonic ischemia occurs at watersheds (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid junction), causing crampy pain then hematochezia with a thumbprint sign in older adults.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Other intestinal disorders: ischemia, angiodysplasia, ileus, obstruction, SIBO
vignette: A 58-year-old woman is evaluated 2 days after abdominal surgery for decreased flatus and constipation. Her abdomen is distended and tympanic, and bowel sounds are markedly decreased. Imaging shows dilated loops of bowel diffusely with no transition zone or air-fluid levels. She has been receiving opiates for pain and has a serum potassium of 3.0 mEq/L.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's findings?

options.text: Adhesive small bowel obstruction with a transition zone
Acute mesenteric ischemia from an embolic SMA occlusion
Sigmoid volvulus with a coffee bean sign
Adynamic ileus from postoperative state, opiates, and hypokalemia
Colonic ischemia at the splenic flexure

explanation_correct: Ileus is intestinal hypomotility without obstruction, producing constipation, decreased flatus, a distended tympanic abdomen, and decreased bowel sounds. There is no transition zone on imaging. It is associated with abdominal surgery, opiates, hypokalemia, and sepsis, and is treated with bowel rest, electrolyte correction, and cholinergic drugs. This patient has multiple of these risk factors.

explanation_incorrect.A: Adhesive small bowel obstruction causes pain, vomiting, and air-fluid levels with a transition zone, not diffuse hypomotility with decreased bowel sounds and no transition zone.
explanation_incorrect.B: Acute mesenteric ischemia causes pain out of proportion to exam and currant jelly stools from SMA embolism, not postoperative hypomotility with decreased flatus.
explanation_incorrect.C: Sigmoid volvulus causes a coffee bean-shaped dilated loop and obstruction, not the diffuse, transition-zone-free dilation of adynamic ileus.
explanation_incorrect.E: Colonic ischemia at the splenic flexure causes crampy pain and hematochezia with a thumbprint sign, not painless postoperative hypomotility and hypokalemia.

educationalObjective: Ileus is hypomotility without obstruction, with decreased flatus and bowel sounds and no transition zone, often after surgery, opiates, or hypokalemia.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Other intestinal disorders: ischemia, angiodysplasia, ileus, obstruction, SIBO
vignette: A 5-day-old infant born at 28 weeks' gestation, fed formula, develops abdominal distention, bloody stools, and lethargy. Abdominal radiographs show gas within the bowel wall and a bubbly appearance, along with gas in the portal venous system. The terminal ileum and proximal colon are most severely affected.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hirschsprung disease with an aganglionic distal colon
Intussusception with a Meckel diverticulum lead point
Necrotizing enterocolitis
Midgut volvulus from malrotation
Meconium ileus from a meconium plug

explanation_correct: Necrotizing enterocolitis is seen in premature, formula-fed infants with immature immune systems and involves necrosis of intestinal mucosa, most commonly the terminal ileum and proximal colon. It produces pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in the bowel wall), pneumoperitoneum, and portal venous gas—the bubbly radiographic pattern and portal gas described here. Bloody stools, distention, and lethargy are typical.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hirschsprung disease causes failure to pass meconium and an aganglionic distal colon with a transition zone, not pneumatosis and portal venous gas in a premature infant.
explanation_incorrect.B: Intussusception causes intermittent pain, currant jelly stools, and a target sign in older infants, not bowel wall gas and portal venous gas.
explanation_incorrect.D: Midgut volvulus from malrotation causes bilious vomiting and twisting around the mesentery, not pneumatosis intestinalis in a premature formula-fed infant.
explanation_incorrect.E: Meconium ileus from a meconium plug causes neonatal obstruction (classically with cystic fibrosis), not the intestinal necrosis with portal venous gas seen here.

educationalObjective: Necrotizing enterocolitis affects premature formula-fed infants with terminal ileal/proximal colonic necrosis, pneumatosis, and portal venous gas.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Other intestinal disorders: ischemia, angiodysplasia, ileus, obstruction, SIBO
vignette: A 45-year-old man presents with abrupt onset of colicky abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal distention. He has had two prior laparotomies. An upright abdominal x-ray shows dilated loops of small bowel proximal to the obstruction with air-fluid levels and collapsed bowel distally. He is hypotensive with dry mucous membranes.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause and initial management of this patient's condition?

options.text: Intraperitoneal adhesions; gastrointestinal decompression, volume resuscitation, and bowel rest
Acolonic false diverticulum; urgent sigmoid resection
Embolic SMA occlusion; immediate angiographic embolectomy
Adynamic ileus; bowel rest and electrolyte correction alone
Angiodysplasia of the right colon; colonoscopic cauterization

explanation_correct: Small bowel obstruction interrupts the normal flow of intraluminal contents, causing fluid accumulation and dilation proximal to the blockage with decompression distal to it. It presents with abrupt pain, nausea, vomiting, and distention, and upright x-ray shows air-fluid levels. The most common causes are intraperitoneal adhesions, tumors, and hernias; management is gastrointestinal decompression, volume resuscitation, and bowel rest. Prior laparotomies make adhesions most likely here.

explanation_incorrect.B: A colonic false diverticulum relates to diverticulosis or diverticulitis of the sigmoid, not a small bowel obstruction with air-fluid levels after laparotomies.
explanation_incorrect.C: Embolic SMA occlusion causes acute mesenteric ischemia with pain out of proportion, not mechanical obstruction with air-fluid levels and proximal dilation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Adynamic ileus has no transition zone or air-fluid levels and features decreased bowel sounds; this patient has colicky pain and a mechanical obstruction pattern after surgeries.
explanation_incorrect.E: Angiodysplasia causes painless hematochezia from right colon vessels, not an obstructive picture with vomiting, distention, and air-fluid levels.

educationalObjective: Small bowel obstruction is most often caused by adhesions, tumors, or hernias and is managed with decompression, volume resuscitation, and bowel rest.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Other intestinal disorders: ischemia, angiodysplasia, ileus, obstruction, SIBO
vignette: A 55-year-old man with a history of gastric bypass surgery and long-term proton pump inhibitor use presents with bloating, flatulence, abdominal pain, and chronic watery diarrhea. He has macrocytic anemia from vitamin B12 malabsorption. He also has a history of HIV with low CD4 count. A carbohydrate breath test is abnormally positive early.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's findings and the basis for the diagnostic test?

options.text: Colonic ischemia at the rectosigmoid junction with bacterial translocation
Chronic mesenteric ischemia from celiac artery atherosclerosis
Acute mesenteric ischemia from SMA embolization with bowel necrosis
Adynamic ileus with hypomotility and bacterial stasis
Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth with carbohydrate fermentation; the breath test detects early hydrogen production

explanation_correct: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth occurs with altered pH (achlorhydria, PPI use), anatomic changes (gastric bypass, blind loop, obstruction, fistula), dysmotility, and immune deficiency (IgA deficiency, HIV). Bacteria ferment ingested carbohydrate early in the small bowel, producing hydrogen that is detected by an abnormally early rise on a carbohydrate breath test; severe cases cause vitamin B12 malabsorption. This patient has multiple risk factors and a positive breath test.

explanation_incorrect.A: Colonic ischemia at the rectosigmoid watershed causes crampy pain and hematochezia with a thumbprint sign, not bloating and B12 malabsorption with a positive breath test.
explanation_incorrect.B: Chronic mesenteric ischemia causes postprandial epigastric pain with food aversion and weight loss from atherosclerosis, not chronic watery diarrhea and an early positive carbohydrate breath test.
explanation_incorrect.C: Acute mesenteric ischemia from SMA embolism causes severe pain out of proportion and currant jelly stools, not the bloating, flatulence, and B12 malabsorption described.
explanation_incorrect.D: Adynamic ileus has decreased flatus and bowel sounds without a transition zone; it does not cause the early carbohydrate fermentation and B12 malabsorption of bacterial overgrowth.

educationalObjective: SIBO is promoted by PPI use, anatomic bypass/blind loop, dysmotility, and HIV/IgA deficiency, causing bloating, diarrhea, and B12 malabsorption diagnosed by breath test.
